DENIAL MANAGEMENT

Why Family Medicine Claims Get Denied And How PMEX Eliminates Each Root Cause

Family medicine denials are high-volume and low-visibility. E/M downcoding, AWV billing errors, and CCM documentation gaps each repeat across hundreds of claims before anyone catches them. PMEX resolves them at the workflow level, not claim by claim.

Denial Resubmission Turnaround

PATTERN 01

Payer Downcodes 99214 to 99213 — Systematically

Practice bills 99214 for an established patient with diabetes, hypertension, and a new complaint. UnitedHealthcare auto-downcodes to 99213 — their algorithm finds the documentation does not clearly separate the chronic disease management from the new complaint complexity. $38 lost per visit. Across 50 visits per day, that is $70,000 annually in systematic downcoding.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX reviews every 99214 and 99215 against 2021 AMA MDM criteria before submission and adds appropriate documentation cues when notes support a higher level but lack the specific MDM language payers' algorithms look for. When a payer downcodes a correctly supported claim, PMEX appeals with MDM documentation and tracks the pattern across all future similar claims.

PATTERN 02

Annual Wellness Visit Billed as Preventive Physical — Wrong Code

Medicare patient comes in for Annual Wellness Visit. Practice bills 99395 (routine preventive physical). Medicare denies — the AWV benefit is specifically G0438/G0439 and does not cover routine physicals under the same benefit. Patient receives a bill they should not have. Claim sits in AR uncollected.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX identifies AWV encounters from visit type and documentation, applies G0438 (initial) or G0439 (subsequent), and manages the same-day E/M plus AWV combination per CMS guidance. No Medicare preventive revenue lost to AWV-versus-physical coding errors.

PATTERN 03

CCM Claim Denied — 20-Minute Threshold Not Documented

Practice launches CCM billing. 99490 submitted monthly for 150 patients. Aetna requests documentation for 12 patients — time logs are incomplete, the care coordinator's notes are missing, the care plan was not updated this month. 12 claims denied simultaneously. Practice is not sure how to reconstruct the documentation.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX maintains monthly CCM time tracking documentation for every enrolled patient — care coordinator time logs, care plan update records, and patient contact notes — in a format that satisfies payer audit requests. No CCM claim is submitted without a complete monthly time record attached.

PATTERN 04

Same-Day E/M and Preventive Visit — E/M Denied as Bundled

Patient comes in for annual physical. Physician also addresses a new hypertension medication change in the same visit. E/M (99214) billed same day as preventive (99395). No Modifier 25. Payer bundles the E/M into the preventive visit and denies the E/M — $115 to $155 per visit lost. Pattern repeats across every same-day E/M plus preventive combination.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX applies Modifier 25 on the E/M code whenever a separately identifiable medical problem is addressed on the same day as a preventive service. Documentation confirmed before submission. No same-day combination claim leaves the office without the correct modifier applied.

PATTERN 05

Transitional Care Claim Denied — 2-Day Contact Not Documented

Patient discharged from hospital. TCM billed (99496). Payer requests documentation of the required two-day interactive contact with the patient. Practice cannot locate the contact record — it was a verbal phone call with no note in the EHR. Claim denied. $267 per episode permanently lost.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX generates a documentation requirement for every TCM episode at the time of discharge notification — alerting clinical staff to complete and log the two-day contact with a structured EHR note. Every TCM claim is submitted with a documented contact record that satisfies payer audit standards.

PATTERN 06

Rural Health Clinic Claims at Wrong Rate or Wrong Form

RHC submits claims using CMS-1500 at the standard physician fee schedule. RHC services should be billed on UB-04 at the all-inclusive rate using T1015. Or: a non-RHC-qualifying service is billed at the RHC rate, triggering payer audit of the entire RHC billing relationship.

PMEX SOLUTION

PMEX manages RHC billing as a dedicated workflow — UB-04 form, T1015 encounter code, all-inclusive rate structure, and cost report reconciliation. Services that do not qualify under the RHC benefit are correctly routed to the physician fee schedule. Zero RHC form or rate errors on PMEX-managed rural health clinic claims.

THE EDUCATION

What Makes Family Medicine Billing in the USA Harder Than It Looks

Family medicine generates the highest claim volume of any outpatient specialty in U.S. healthcare and the revenue optimization opportunities hiding in that volume are more significant than most practices realize.

Family medicine billing is the process of coding and submitting insurance claims for comprehensive primary care services office visits, preventive care, chronic disease management, minor procedures, behavioral health integration, and care coordination. The billing complexity of primary care is not in the procedure codes it is in the visit-level coding decisions and chronic care program capture that happen on every single patient encounter.

The 2021 AMA E/M guideline changes fundamentally restructured how office visits are coded for established patients. Complexity is now determined by either medical decision-making complexity or total physician time replacing the multi-component history, exam, and MDM system. Most family medicine practices made surface-level changes to their documentation workflows but have not fully optimized their E/M level distribution under the new guidelines. The result: established patient visits systematically coded at level 3 (99213, $100-$115) when the clinical documentation actually supports level 4 (99214, $138-$155) or level 5 (99215, $194-$220).

The three largest untapped revenue programs in U.S. family medicine are Chronic Care Management (CCM, CPT 99490), which generates recurring monthly revenue for coordinating care in patients with two or more chronic conditions; Transitional Care Management (TCM, CPT 99495/99496), which pays $198 to $267 per hospital discharge for care coordination your physicians are likely already providing informally; and Annual Wellness Visit coding (AWV, G0438/G0439), which is a Medicare-specific preventive visit often miscoded as a routine physical, resulting in lost reimbursement or patient confusion about cost-sharing.

Value-based care contracts HEDIS measure performance, PCMH recognition, ACO shared savings add a fourth layer of financial complexity that directly affects revenue through bonuses, penalties, and risk adjustment factors. PMEX tracks quality measure performance alongside billing to help family practices maximize both fee-for-service revenue and value-based incentives from the same clinical documentation.

THE BIGGEST MISSED REVENUE IN U.S PSYCHIATRIC BILLING

The Psychiatric E/M + 90833 Add-On Trap:
How U.S Psychiatrists Leave $100K to $450K Per Year on the Table Without Knowing It

When a U.S. psychiatrist provides medication management (an E/M service) and also performs psychotherapy during the same session, U.S. payer rules allow billing for both services. The E/M code (99213, 99214, 99215) covers the medical decision-making. Add-on code 90833 (30-minute psychotherapy), 90836 (45-minute), or 90838 (60-minute) covers the therapy time.

The catch: both services must be separately documented in the clinical note. The E/M portion must be significant and separately identifiable from the psychotherapy. Most psychiatrists perform both services in a combined note format which is clinically fine but creates a billing gap because the coder cannot identify the two separate elements to bill both codes.

PMEX trains on psychiatric note formats. Our specialists recognize the dual-service structure in a combined note, extract the separately billable elements, and apply the correct add-on code recovering between $98 and $162 per session that would otherwise go unbilled. For a psychiatrist seeing 20 combined sessions per week, that is $100K to $168K recovered annually from visits that already happened.

MARKET INTELLIGENCE

U.S. Mental Health Billing in
2025: Numbers That Matter

Mental health is the fastest-growing outpatient specialty in U.S. healthcare driven by a documented mental health crisis, permanent telehealth expansion, and federal parity enforcement that is beginning to produce real consequences for non-compliant payers.

The billing opportunity is hiding in plain sight. Most U.S. psychiatric practices are collecting 60 to 70 cents of every billable dollar because they do not recognize the E/M plus psychotherapy add-on billing opportunity, do not allocate psychological testing units correctly, and do not code inpatient subsequent care at the level the documentation supports. None of these problems require new patients they require better billing of existing visits.

The denial environment is also intensifying. Regence, Premera, Molina, Healthfirst, and state Medicaid MCOs have tightened medical necessity documentation requirements for inpatient psychiatric claims. Practices that relied on simple daily note submission without clinical justification for length of stay are seeing denial rates climb. PMEX manages medical necessity documentation review as part of every inpatient billing workflow.

Common Questions

Mental Health Billing Answered

Everything you need to know about PMEX mental health billing services

CPT 90833 is a psychotherapy add-on code for 30 minutes of individual psychotherapy when performed on the same day as an E/M service by the same physician. CPT 90836 covers 45 minutes and 90838 covers 60 minutes. When a psychiatrist does both medication management (billable as an E/M code 99213-99215) and psychotherapy in the same session, both the E/M and the add-on code can be billed. Most psychiatrists are not billing this because their billing team either does not recognize the dual-service structure in a combined note, or is not trained to separate the two components for billing purposes. PMEX reads psychiatric notes to identify every qualifying session and applies the correct add-on code. The average value per missed add-on is $98 to $162 per session.

To bill an E/M code plus psychotherapy add-on in the same session, the clinical note must document two separately identifiable services. The E/M portion must show medical decision-making or total provider time attributable to the medical evaluation and management work. The psychotherapy portion must document the psychotherapy minutes separately and show that interactive, face-to-face psychotherapy was provided. The two elements do not need to be in separate note sections PMEX specialists are trained to identify both elements within a combined psychiatric note format and extract the separately billable components.

PMEX manages the full psychological testing billing workflow. 96130 and 96131 cover psychologist evaluation, interpretation, and feedback each requires documented psychologist face-to-face time. 96136 and 96137 cover technician-administered test administration 30 minutes per unit, with a documented list of instruments administered. Prior authorization is verified against actual planned testing hours before the battery begins. The interpretation documentation is reviewed for completeness before the claim is submitted. Common errors missing the interpretation code, incorrect unit counts, auth mismatch against actual hours are eliminated before the claim leaves the office.

CPT 99231 is subsequent hospital care requiring a problem-focused interval history and examination with straightforward medical decision-making. CPT 99232 requires an expanded problem-focused interval history and examination with moderate complexity MDM. CPT 99233 requires a detailed interval history and examination with high complexity MDM. The code level must be selected based on the documented content of the daily note not the physician's preference or a system default. PMEX reviews each inpatient note and selects the level the documentation actually supports. Most psychiatric practices billing 99231 for all days have documentation that supports 99232 or 99233 on 50 to 70% of admission days.

PMEX applies the correct telehealth modifier and place of service for each payer on every mental health telehealth claim. Medicare requires modifier 95 with POS 02 for audio-video sessions at a telehealth originating site, or POS 10 for patient-home sessions. Audio-only requires modifier FQ where covered. Commercial payers have individual telehealth coverage rules that PMEX maps and updates continuously UnitedHealthcare, Aetna, Cigna, BCBS, and all state Medicaid programs. No systematic telehealth denials from modifier or POS mismatches on any PMEX client.

PMEX manages the full spectrum of mental health billing within one engagement psychiatric E/M and add-on billing for psychiatrists and PMHNPs, time-based psychotherapy CPT coding for therapists and social workers, and psychological testing billing for psychologists. Each billing scenario is handled by specialists trained in that specific code set. PMEX identifies carve-out behavioral health plans at eligibility verification Optum Behavioral Health, Magellan Health, and Beacon Health Options are the most common carve-out entities in the U.S. market. When a patient's mental health benefits are managed separately from their medical plan, PMEX routes the claim to the correct carve-out entity. This eliminates a denial category that most mental health practices do not recognize as having a systematic cause they see the denial, resubmit to the same wrong payer, and get denied again.

Yes. PMEX bills PHP (partial hospitalization program) using HCPCS H0035 and G0129 depending on payer, and IOP (intensive outpatient program) using H0015 and applicable procedure codes. Medical necessity documentation, prior authorization, and level-of-care criteria are verified before each PHP and IOP billing cycle. Step-down notifications to payers are managed as clinical level of care changes, preventing authorization gaps during the transition from inpatient to PHP to IOP to outpatient.

PMEX manages PMHNP billing under the provider's own NPI once credentialed, and handles the supervision documentation billing under the supervising psychiatrist's NPI during the interim credentialing period. Supervision documentation requirements vary by payer some require co-signature on the note, others accept a supervision attestation statement, others bill incident-to under Medicare. PMEX tracks each payer's requirement and applies the correct billing approach for each PMHNP on your staff while individual credentialing is processed.

PMEX audits 90 days of prior claims before transitioning, identifies the top billing gaps, and implements corrections from the first claim submitted. Full AR stabilization typically takes 60 to 90 days. PMEX tracks prior authorization requirements, session limits, and medical necessity criteria by payer for mental health versus equivalent medical services.
